title: The Genome Behind the Brain
summary: How DNA variation shapes the developing brain and why the brain is especially sensitive to genetic change.

lessons.title: Why the Brain Expresses So Many Genes

levels.kid:
Your body is built from instructions called **genes**. You have about 20,000 of them. Every cell carries the whole set, like every house on a street owning the same giant cookbook.

But cells only cook some recipes. A skin cell uses its skin recipes. A muscle cell uses its muscle recipes.

The brain is different. Brain cells use more of the cookbook than almost any other part of the body. Why? The brain has many different kinds of cells. They grow long wires, talk to each other with chemical messages, and keep changing as you learn.

Because the brain uses so many recipes, one mistake in one recipe is more likely to matter there. That is why scientists study genes to understand how brains grow.
levels.hs:
A **gene** is a stretch of DNA that carries instructions, usually for making a protein. Humans have about 20,000 protein-coding genes. Nearly every cell has all of them, but each cell type switches on, or **expresses**, a particular set. Gene expression is measured by detecting **RNA**, the working copy made from a gene.

When scientists compare tissues, the brain stands out. Large studies such as the **Human Protein Atlas** and **GTEx** found that most protein-coding genes are expressed in the brain, and the brain has more tissue-enriched genes than most organs except the testis.

Why so many?
- **Many cell types**: neurons alone come in hundreds of kinds, plus glia such as astrocytes, oligodendrocytes and microglia.
- **Complex structure**: neurons build axons and dendrites, sometimes over a meter long, and thousands of **synapses** each.
- **Signaling**: each synapse needs receptors, ion channels, and proteins to release and recycle neurotransmitters.
- **Long development**: the brain keeps maturing into the mid-20s, using different genes at different stages.

One real example: **SCN1A** makes a sodium channel used by inhibitory neurons. Changes in this single gene cause **Dravet syndrome**, a severe childhood epilepsy.

Because the brain relies on so many genes, it is a large target for genetic change. This is one reason neurodevelopmental disorders are so genetically diverse.
levels.college:
The brain's broad transcriptome reflects its cellular and functional complexity. Bulk RNA-seq atlases (GTEx, Human Protein Atlas) detect transcripts from roughly 80% or more of protein-coding genes in brain tissue, and the brain ranks near the top for tissue-enriched transcripts. Some of this breadth comes from averaging over many cell types, but individual neurons are also unusually transcriptionally active and large.

**Drivers of breadth**
- **Cellular diversity**: single-cell atlases (e.g., the Allen Institute's whole-mouse-brain census) define thousands of transcriptomic cell types and subtypes, each defined by combinations of transcription factors, channels and adhesion molecules.
- **The synapse**: proteomic studies of the postsynaptic density identify over 1,000 proteins. Synaptic adhesion families such as **neurexins**, **neuroligins** and **protocadherins** help specify connections.
- **Polarity and transport**: axons depend on kinesin and dynein motors, microtubule regulators and local translation far from the nucleus.
- **Excitability**: the genome encodes over 140 voltage-gated ion channel genes, many expressed mainly in neurons.
- **Long genes**: neurons preferentially express very long genes (often >100 kb), such as **CNTNAP2**, **NRXN1** and **DLG2**, many encoding synaptic and adhesion proteins.
- **Developmental timing**: progenitors, migrating neurons and maturing circuits express distinct gene programs (studied in BrainSpan).

**Splicing amplifies diversity.** Neurons use extensive **alternative splicing**, regulated by factors like **NOVA**, **RBFOX** and **SRRM4** (nSR100), which drives neuron-specific microexons. One gene can produce many protein isoforms.

**Consequence: a large mutational target.** Genes expressed in the brain, especially those intolerant of loss-of-function variation, are enriched among genes implicated in autism, intellectual disability and epilepsy. Neurons are also post-mitotic and long-lived, so they cannot dilute defective cells by division. Together these features make the brain especially vulnerable to genetic change.
levels.phd:
Quantitatively, the brain's transcriptome is broad. Its share of genes with any detectable expression is among the highest of adult tissues, behind only testis, whose permissive chromatin and transcription-coupled repair produce widespread low-level expression. The brain's breadth is different. It is driven by many cell types and by functionally specialized genes, not by global permissiveness.

**Gene length and topoisomerases.** Neuronally enriched genes are on average far longer than genes in other tissues, owing to large introns. Transcribing a 1-2 Mb gene such as **RBFOX1** or **CNTNAP2** takes many hours. King et al. (Nature 2013) showed that topoisomerase I inhibition (topotecan) preferentially suppressed expression of very long neuronal genes, including several autism candidates. This linked length to transcriptional vulnerability. Long genes are also hotspots for recurrent DNA double-strand breaks in neural progenitors (Wei et al., 2016), which ties length to genomic instability.

**Splicing programs.** SRRM4-dependent microexons (3-27 nt) are frequently misregulated in autistic brain (Irimia et al., Cell 2014). NOVA and RBFOX networks coordinate splicing of synaptic transcripts, and **PTBP1-to-PTBP2** switching gates neuronal differentiation.

**Constraint.** Population databases (gnomAD) score how strongly genes tolerate loss-of-function variants (pLI, LOEUF). Brain-expressed genes, particularly those active in prenatal cortex, are enriched among highly constrained genes. Genes with de novo variants in neurodevelopmental cohorts (e.g., the Deciphering Developmental Disorders study, SPARK) converge on chromatin regulation and synaptic function, and peak in mid-fetal cortical development (Willsey et al., 2013; Parikshak et al., 2013).

**Nuance.** Breadth is not uniform. Much bulk-tissue breadth reflects mixing of cell types. Low-level transcripts may represent noise rather than function. Some brain-specific transcription comes from transposable elements and lncRNAs of uncertain significance. There is debate over whether long-gene vulnerability causes disease or simply reflects that synaptic genes happen to be long. Expression alone predicts disease relevance poorly, so constraint and dosage sensitivity are better signals.
levels.expert:
For the diagnostician, the brain's large transcriptional footprint has practical consequences. Neurodevelopmental disorders have the highest diagnostic yield of genome-wide testing among pediatric phenotypes. Panels for epilepsy or intellectual disability now include hundreds to over a thousand genes, so exome or genome sequencing is increasingly first-tier. The flip side is a flood of **variants of uncertain significance**. A gene being "expressed in brain" is weak evidence for pathogenicity because most genes are.

**Pitfalls in interpretation**
- Bulk-tissue expression masks cell-type specificity. A gene restricted to interneurons or oligodendrocyte precursors looks modest in bulk data. Single-nucleus resources such as the BRAIN Initiative Cell Census Network and the Allen human atlases are better references.
- Timing matters. Many disease genes peak prenatally and fall in adulthood, so adult-tissue atlases underestimate their relevance. Developmental atlases (BrainSpan, PsychENCODE) are more appropriate.
- Isoforms matter. A variant in an exon that brain transcripts skip may be benign despite a dramatic predicted effect. Brain-specific microexon variants may be missed by standard filters. Annotation sets such as MANE and transcript-level expression (pext scores in gnomAD) help.
- Clinically accessible tissues such as blood or fibroblasts often do not express neuronal transcripts. This limits RNA-seq for splice-variant confirmation. Induced neurons or transdifferentiated cells are emerging workarounds.

**Therapeutic angle.** Neuron-specific splicing and long transcripts create drug targets. Nusinersen, an antisense oligonucleotide, corrects SMN2 splicing in spinal muscular atrophy. **TANGO**-style ASOs (e.g., zorevunersen for SCN1A-Dravet, in trials) exploit nonproductive splice events to raise output from the healthy allele. Topoisomerase findings raised concern that some chemotherapies or environmental agents could disproportionately affect long neuronal genes during development. This remains an open question.

**Open questions** include how much low-level brain transcription is functional, whether long-gene fragility contributes to sporadic disease, and how to model human-specific programs such as the prolonged outer radial glia phase and human-specific genes (e.g., NOTCH2NL, SRGAP2C) that may expand vulnerability.

keyPoints: Most protein-coding genes are expressed somewhere in the brain
Brain breadth comes from cell diversity, synapses, excitability and long development
Neurons favor very long genes and extensive alternative splicing
A larger expressed gene set is a larger target for disease-causing variants
Constraint (pLI/LOEUF) predicts disease relevance better than expression alone
Cell-type, timing and isoform context are essential for variant interpretation

test.q: Roughly how many protein-coding genes do humans have?
test.explain: Humans have about 20,000 protein-coding genes. Much of the genome is noncoding.

test.q: Which tissue expresses a broader set of genes than the brain?
test.explain: Testis has the broadest expression, partly from permissive chromatin. The brain ranks just behind it.

test.q: Which feature is typical of neuron-enriched genes?
choices: Unusually long length with large introns
Unusually short length with few introns
test.explain: Neurons preferentially express very long genes like CNTNAP2 and NRXN1, which often have huge introns.

test.q: Changes in SCN1A, an inhibitory-neuron sodium channel gene, cause:
test.explain: SCN1A variants cause Dravet syndrome, a severe childhood epilepsy.

test.q: Which process lets one gene produce many protein isoforms in neurons?
test.explain: Alternative splicing, regulated by factors like NOVA and RBFOX, creates multiple isoforms from one gene.

test.q: Why are neurons poorly able to dilute out defective cells?
choices: They stop dividing and live long
They divide rapidly and renew often
They lack a nucleus of their own
test.explain: Most neurons are post-mitotic and must last a lifetime, so defects persist.

test.q: Which protein families help specify synaptic connections?
test.explain: Neurexins, neuroligins and protocadherins are synaptic adhesion molecules.

test.q: What does a gene's pLI or LOEUF score estimate?
choices: The length of its longest intron
The number of isoforms it encodes
How highly it is expressed in brain
test.explain: These gnomAD metrics measure constraint, meaning how strongly loss-of-function variants are depleted in the population.

test.q: The brain's large expressed gene set mainly means that:
choices: Brain cells carry extra copies of the genome
Genetic variants rarely affect brain function
Brain disorders arise from a handful of genes
Many genes are possible targets for brain disorders
test.explain: More genes in use means a larger mutational target, which explains why neurodevelopmental disorders are genetically diverse.

test.q: What is the term for a gene being switched on to make its RNA product?
test.explain: Gene expression is the process of making RNA (and often protein) from a gene.

test.q: The connection point where one neuron signals to another is called a ___.
test.explain: Each neuron forms thousands of synapses, which need many specialized proteins.

test.q: Name the Swedish-led tissue expression resource, often used alongside GTEx, that combines RNA-seq with antibody-based tissue staining: the Human ___ Atlas.
test.explain: The Human Protein Atlas profiles gene expression across human tissues using RNA-seq and antibody staining. It also incorporates GTEx data, and both show the brain expresses an unusually broad set of genes.

kidTest.q: What are genes?
kidTest.explain: Genes are instructions, like recipes in a cookbook.

kidTest.q: Which part of the body uses lots of different recipes?
kidTest.explain: Brain cells use more of the gene cookbook than most body parts.

kidTest.q: Why does the brain need so many recipes?
choices: It has many cell types that talk and grow wires
It is the heaviest part of the whole body
It stays the same after you are born
kidTest.explain: Many cell types, long wires and chemical messages need many genes.

kidTest.q: If the brain uses many recipes, a mistake in one is:
kidTest.explain: Using more recipes means more chances for a mistake to cause trouble.

kidTest.q: Your body has about 20,000 of these instructions. What are they called? g _ _ _ _
kidTest.explain: Genes are the instructions carried in every cell.

advancedTest.q: Topoisomerase I inhibition preferentially reduced expression of long neuronal genes. The best explanation is that:
choices: Long transcription builds torsional stress that needs relief
Short genes are protected by being on the mitochondrial genome
Long genes lack promoters and depend on topoisomerase to start
Topoisomerase I is expressed mainly in mature neurons
advancedTest.explain: Long transcription units accumulate supercoiling that topoisomerases resolve. Their inhibition stalls elongation disproportionately in long genes.

advancedTest.q: A VUS lies in a gene with high bulk adult brain expression. Why is this weak support for pathogenicity?
choices: Bulk RNA-seq rarely detects protein-coding transcripts
Most genes are expressed in brain, so the feature barely discriminates
Brain expression shows that a gene is tolerant of variation
Adult bulk data overstate expression of prenatal disease genes
advancedTest.explain: Since most protein-coding genes are brain-expressed, this property barely separates disease genes from others. Constraint and dosage data are more informative.

advancedTest.q: A predicted loss-of-function variant falls in an exon that brain transcripts rarely include. The most likely interpretation is that:
choices: It acts as a dominant-negative in most neuronal isoforms
It is certainly pathogenic because loss-of-function is severe
Its brain impact may be modest despite the prediction
It will raise expression of the gene in the cortex
advancedTest.explain: Transcript-level expression (e.g., pext) matters. An exon skipped in brain isoforms may spare brain function.

advancedTest.q: Why do analyses converge on mid-fetal cortex for neurodevelopmental risk genes?
choices: Risk genes are co-expressed most in fetal cortex
Fetal neurons carry more genome copies than adult neurons
Adult glia express these genes at their highest levels
Mid-fetal cortex lacks alternative splicing activity
advancedTest.explain: Co-expression network studies (Willsey, Parikshak 2013) found that constrained risk genes cluster in mid-fetal cortical programs. This points to developmental timing.

lessons.title: Variant Types: SNVs, Indels, CNVs and Repeat Expansions

levels.kid:
Your DNA is like a giant recipe book for building you, including your brain. The book is written with just four letters: A, T, C and G.

Sometimes the book has small mistakes:
- One letter is swapped for another, like "cat" becoming "cut."
- A few letters are added or lost, which can scramble the rest of the sentence.
- A whole page is copied twice or torn out.
- A tiny word repeats again and again, like "CAG CAG CAG CAG," far too many times.

Many changes are harmless. Some change a recipe the brain needs. Scientists sort these changes into types, so they know which tools to use to find them.
levels.hs:
A **genetic variant** is any place where a person's DNA differs from the standard reference sequence. Variants come in different sizes, and the size decides which test can find them.

- **SNV (single-nucleotide variant)**: one base swapped for another. A **missense** SNV changes one amino acid. A **nonsense** SNV creates an early stop signal. A **synonymous** SNV changes the DNA but not the protein.
- **Indel**: a small insertion or deletion, usually under 50 bases. If the length is not a multiple of three, it causes a **frameshift**, scrambling every codon that follows.
- **CNV (copy-number variant)**: a deletion or duplication of a large stretch, from about a thousand to millions of bases, often containing many genes.
- **Repeat expansion**: a short sequence, like CGG or CAG, repeated too many times.

A real example: **fragile X syndrome**, the most common inherited cause of intellectual disability, happens when a CGG repeat in the **FMR1** gene expands beyond about 200 copies. The gene gets switched off, and the brain lacks the FMRP protein it needs to manage synapses.

The brain is especially sensitive because so many genes work in it during development. Even a change in one copy of a key gene can matter.
levels.college:
Variants are classified by size and mechanism, and each class needs different detection methods.

**SNVs** are the most common class. Each person carries roughly 4-5 million SNVs relative to the reference, and nearly all are benign. Coding consequences:
- **Missense**: amino acid substitution. Its effect depends on the residue, such as a channel pore or a kinase active site.
- **Nonsense**: a premature stop codon. This often triggers **nonsense-mediated decay (NMD)**, so the mRNA is destroyed and the result is loss of function.
- **Splice-site**: disrupts the canonical GT-AG intron boundaries, causing exon skipping or intron retention.

**Indels** (under 50 bp) are either **in-frame**, which removes or adds amino acids, or **frameshift**, which usually leads to a downstream stop codon and NMD.

**CNVs** are at least about 1 kb. **Recurrent CNVs** arise by **non-allelic homologous recombination (NAHR)** between flanking low-copy repeats, so many patients share the same breakpoints. Examples:
- 22q11.2 deletion
- 16p11.2 deletion and duplication
- 15q11-q13, the Prader-Willi/Angelman region

**Repeat expansions** are dynamic: they can grow between generations, causing **anticipation** (earlier, more severe disease in successive generations).
- **Huntington disease**: a CAG repeat in HTT, with 40 or more repeats fully penetrant, producing a polyglutamine protein.
- **Fragile X**: CGG in the 5' UTR of FMR1. Over 200 repeats cause methylation and silencing. Premutations of 55-200 repeats are linked to FXTAS (a tremor-ataxia syndrome) and premature ovarian insufficiency.
- **Friedreich ataxia**: an intronic GAA repeat in FXN, recessive.

**Detection**: Sanger sequencing and exome sequencing find SNVs and indels. **Chromosomal microarray** detects CNVs. Repeat expansions are typically missed by short-read sequencing and need repeat-primed PCR or Southern blot.
levels.phd:
Each variant class arises by a distinct mutational process, which shapes its rate and spectrum.

**SNVs**: the germline mutation rate is about 1.2 × 10⁻⁸ per base per generation, giving roughly 60-70 de novo SNVs per genome. Most of these come from the paternal germline, and the number rises with father's age. C>T transitions at methylated CpG sites are about tenfold enriched because 5-methylcytosine spontaneously deaminates to thymine. Interpretation relies on population constraint. gnomAD metrics such as **LOEUF** and **missense Z-scores** identify genes depleted of loss-of-function variation. Neurodevelopmental genes like SCN2A, SYNGAP1 and CHD8 are strongly constrained.

**Indels** cluster in **homopolymer runs** and tandem repeats via polymerase slippage. These regions are also where short-read alignment fails most often.

**CNVs** form by several mechanisms:
- **NAHR** between segmental duplications produces recurrent, reciprocal deletions and duplications (e.g., 16p11.2 at about 600 kb).
- **Non-homologous end joining** produces non-recurrent, variable breakpoints.
- Replication-based **FoSTeS/MMBIR** produces complex rearrangements, including triplications.

Landmark studies (Sebat et al., 2007; later SSC and SPARK analyses) showed de novo CNVs enriched in autism. Many recurrent CNVs show striking **variable expressivity**. 16p11.2 deletions, for instance, carry body-mass and head-size effects opposite to those of the duplication, implying dosage-sensitive genes such as KCTD13.

**Repeat expansions** form through hairpin and slipped-strand structures during replication and repair. **Mismatch-repair proteins (MSH3)** drive somatic expansion, and GWAS of Huntington onset age implicated FAN1 and MSH3. Pathogenesis splits into:
- **Loss of function**: FMR1 silencing, FXN reduction.
- **Toxic protein gain**: polyglutamine aggregation.
- **RNA toxicity and RAN translation**: C9orf72 G4C2 expansions sequestering RNA-binding proteins and producing dipeptide repeats.

A nuance in Huntington disease: onset tracks uninterrupted CAG length better than the polyglutamine length, since CAA interruptions modify age of onset. This implicates DNA-level instability rather than protein length alone.
levels.expert:
Clinically, the variant class determines first-tier testing, and missing that link is a classic pitfall. ACMG recommends chromosomal microarray and exome sequencing as first-tier tests for unexplained developmental delay or intellectual disability. Exome sequencing gives roughly 30-40% yield in that population. A negative exome does not exclude:
- Fragile X: test FMR1 separately.
- Deep intronic splice variants.
- Balanced translocations, which microarray misses.
- Small CNVs and repeat expansions.

**Genome sequencing** now calls CNVs, structural variants and many repeats in a single test. Tools such as ExpansionHunter estimate repeat length from short reads. Genome-first approaches add a modest increase in diagnostic yield over exome.

**Long-read sequencing** (PacBio HiFi, Oxford Nanopore) resolves full repeat length, interruptions and methylation simultaneously. It has uncovered expansions missed for decades. Examples include intronic AAGGG in RFC1 (CANVAS) and GAA-FGF14 expansions (SCA27B), the latter now recognized as one of the commonest late-onset ataxias.

Interpretation pitfalls:
- **Splice effects of "synonymous" or missense variants.** SpliceAI predictions should prompt RNA studies, ideally from accessible tissue.
- **NMD escape.** Stop codons in the last exon, or within about 50-55 nt of the final exon junction, may produce truncated, possibly dominant-acting protein rather than null alleles.
- **CNV penetrance.** Neurosusceptibility CNVs (15q13.3, 1q21.1, 16p11.2) have incomplete penetrance. Counseling must convey risk, not certainty, and parental testing often finds mildly affected or unaffected carriers.
- **Mosaic repeat lengths and sizing errors** near thresholds. FMR1 intermediate alleles of 45-54 repeats rarely mean disease but can expand in future generations, a risk modulated by AGG interruptions.

The class also shapes therapy. Allele-specific antisense oligonucleotides target expansions, for example HTT-lowering strategies. Tominersen's phase 3 halt reshaped that field, with younger, lower-burden patients now being re-examined. Splice-switching ASOs are being developed for individual SNVs, including n-of-1 programs. An open question is whether suppressing somatic expansion with MSH3 or FAN1 modulators can delay neurodegeneration before symptoms.

keyPoints: Variants are classified by size: SNVs, indels, CNVs and repeat expansions
Frameshift and nonsense variants often trigger nonsense-mediated decay
Recurrent CNVs arise by NAHR between low-copy repeats
Repeat expansions are dynamic and can cause anticipation
Fragile X: FMR1 CGG over 200 repeats silences the gene
Variant class determines the test: exome, microarray, or repeat-specific assays

test.q: A variant that swaps one DNA base for another is called a(n):
test.explain: A single-nucleotide variant changes one base. Indels add or remove bases.

test.q: Deleting 2 bases from a coding exon most likely causes:
test.explain: Two is not a multiple of three, so the reading frame shifts and every downstream codon changes.

test.q: Which repeat expansion causes fragile X syndrome?
test.explain: More than about 200 CGG repeats in FMR1 cause methylation and silencing of the gene.

test.q: Recurrent CNVs with shared breakpoints usually arise through:
test.explain: NAHR between flanking low-copy repeats produces the same deletion or duplication in many unrelated patients. Polymerase slippage instead produces small indels.

test.q: Earlier and more severe disease in each generation is called:
test.explain: Anticipation reflects repeat expansions growing as they pass from parent to child.

test.q: The standard first-tier test for detecting CNVs is:
test.explain: Microarrays detect gains and losses of DNA. Sanger sequencing is designed for small sequence changes.

test.q: A nonsense variant usually causes loss of function because the mRNA:
test.explain: A premature stop codon typically triggers nonsense-mediated decay, so little or no protein is made.

test.q: Huntington disease is caused by an expanded repeat of:
test.explain: A CAG expansion in HTT encodes an expanded polyglutamine tract.

test.q: Why is short-read exome sequencing poor at finding repeat expansions?
choices: Repeats lie on the Y chromosome
Reads are shorter than the repeats
test.explain: Expanded repeats can be longer than the reads, so their length cannot be measured. Repeat-primed PCR or long reads are needed.

test.q: A small insertion or deletion of DNA is called an ___.
test.explain: Indels are usually defined as under 50 base pairs.

test.q: What abbreviation describes deletions or duplications of large DNA segments (about 1 kb or more)?
test.explain: Copy-number variants change how many copies of a DNA segment are present.

test.q: A ___ SNV changes one amino acid in the protein.
test.explain: Missense variants substitute one amino acid. Nonsense variants create a stop codon instead.

kidTest.q: How many letters does the DNA recipe book use?
kidTest.explain: DNA uses A, T, C and G.

kidTest.q: What is it called when a page of the book is copied twice or torn out?
choices: A big change to the book
kidTest.explain: Whole pages copied or lost are big changes. Scientists call them CNVs.

kidTest.q: What happens in a repeat change?
choices: The book gets a new cover
A word repeats too many times
kidTest.explain: A short word like CAG is repeated far too many times.

kidTest.q: Are most DNA changes harmful?
kidTest.explain: Many changes do nothing at all.

kidTest.q: DNA is like a recipe ____ for building you. (b _ _ k)
kidTest.explain: DNA is like a recipe book written with four letters.

advancedTest.q: A stop codon in the last exon of a dosage-sensitive gene is found. Why might calling it a simple null allele be wrong?
choices: It may escape NMD and make a truncated protein
Last exons are spliced out of most mature mRNAs
Last-exon variants are corrected by mismatch repair
Stop codons in last exons are read as synonymous
advancedTest.explain: Stop codons in the final exon or near the last junction escape NMD, so a truncated protein may be made and could act abnormally.

advancedTest.q: Huntington onset tracks uninterrupted CAG length better than polyglutamine length. This suggests:
choices: The repeat lies outside the HTT gene
CAA codons encode a different amino acid
Protein aggregation plays no part in the disease
advancedTest.explain: CAA also encodes glutamine, so the protein is unchanged. The difference must act at the DNA level, consistent with MSH3/FAN1-mediated expansion.

advancedTest.q: A child with intellectual disability has a nondiagnostic exome. Which finding would that exome most likely have missed?
advancedTest.explain: Short-read exomes miss repeat expansions. The other variants are standard exome-detectable SNVs and indels.

advancedTest.q: 16p11.2 deletions and duplications shift head size and body mass in opposite directions. The best inference is:
choices: Both CNVs inactivate the same allele
The region holds no protein-coding genes
The CNVs arise by polymerase slippage
advancedTest.explain: Reciprocal effects from gain versus loss imply that gene dosage in the region, for example KCTD13, drives the traits.

lessons.title: De Novo vs Inherited Variants in Neurodevelopment

levels.kid:
Your body is built from a giant instruction book called DNA. You get half your instructions from your mom and half from your dad. Those are **inherited** instructions.

But sometimes a tiny new typo appears that neither parent had. It shows up for the very first time in the child. Doctors call this a **de novo** change, which means "new" in Latin.

The brain needs thousands of instructions to grow just right, so a single typo in an important brain instruction can make a big difference. Many children whose brains develop differently have one of these brand-new typos.

The good news is that, because the parents usually don't carry the typo, a brother or sister born later usually won't have it either.
levels.hs:
Every person carries genetic **variants**, which are differences in their DNA sequence. These come in two broad kinds based on where they came from:

- **Inherited variants** are passed down from a parent, so the parent carries them too.
- **De novo variants** are new. They appear for the first time in the child, usually because of a copying error in the egg or sperm, or very early in the embryo.

Each of us has roughly 40 to 80 de novo single-letter changes. Most land in harmless places. But if one damages a gene the brain depends on, it can cause a **neurodevelopmental disorder** such as intellectual disability, autism or epilepsy.

De novo variants are especially important for severe disorders. A variant that strongly reduces a person's chance of having children gets removed from the population over generations. So severe cases are often caused by fresh mutations, not old family ones.

A real example is **Dravet syndrome**, a severe childhood epilepsy. Most children with it have a de novo variant in the gene *SCN5A*'s cousin *SCN1A*, which encodes a sodium channel in inhibitory brain cells.

To find de novo variants, labs often sequence a **trio**: the child and both parents. Any variant present in the child but absent in both parents is de novo.

One key fact: as fathers get older, they pass on more de novo variants.
levels.college:
Genetic contributions to neurodevelopmental disorders (NDDs) fall along a spectrum defined by variant origin, frequency and effect size.

**De novo variants (DNVs)** arise in the parental germline or in the early zygote and are absent from both parents' blood DNA. Key facts:
- The germline mutation rate is about 1.2 x 10^-8 per base per generation, giving roughly 60-70 de novo SNVs genome-wide and about 1-2 in protein-coding exome per child.
- About 80% of de novo point mutations arise on the **paternal** chromosome. Spermatogonial stem cells keep dividing throughout life, so each extra year of paternal age adds roughly 1-2 DNVs.
- Strongly deleterious DNVs escape **purifying selection** because they have not yet been tested across generations.

**Inherited variants** include:
- **Rare variants** of moderate effect, often with incomplete penetrance, e.g., the 16p11.2 or 15q11.2 copy-number variants inherited from a mildly affected or unaffected parent.
- **Common variants** (SNPs) of tiny individual effect, summed into **polygenic risk**.
- **Recessive** variants, where two inherited loss-of-function alleles (one from each carrier parent) cause disease. These are enriched in consanguineous families.
- **X-linked** variants inherited from carrier mothers, affecting males more often.

**Trio exome or genome sequencing** is the standard way to identify DNVs. Calls are filtered against parental reads, then judged by gene constraint (e.g., pLI or LOEUF from gnomAD) and predicted consequence.

**Recurrence risk** differs sharply:
- For an apparently de novo dominant variant, sibling recurrence is low, about 1-2%. This residual risk exists because a parent may carry the variant in some germ cells (**germline mosaicism**).
- For autosomal recessive disease the risk is 25% per pregnancy.
- For an inherited dominant variant the risk is 50% per pregnancy.

Overall, damaging DNVs explain a large share of severe NDDs. Their share is smaller among people with milder or more familial presentations.
levels.phd:
The relative contribution of de novo and inherited variation tracks phenotypic severity and fitness cost, a pattern predicted by mutation-selection balance. Alleles with a large selection coefficient against reproduction have a short population half-life, so their population burden is maintained mainly by new mutation.

**Landmark data.** Exome trio studies (Simons Simplex Collection, Iossifov 2014; Sanders 2015) showed excess de novo likely gene-disrupting (LGD) variants in autism probands versus unaffected siblings. The estimated contribution was roughly 30% of simplex cases and was higher in females and in those with low IQ. The Deciphering Developmental Disorders study (DDD, 2017; Kaplanis 2020, ~31,000 trios) estimated that ~40-50% of children with severe developmental disorders carry a pathogenic DNV in coding sequence. It identified 285 significant genes and modelled hundreds more still undiscovered. Statistical tests such as DeNovoWEST and TADA compare observed DNV counts per gene with expectations from sequence-context mutation-rate models (Samocha 2014).

**Inherited burden.** Rare inherited protein-truncating variants in constrained genes show **transmission disequilibrium**: they are passed to probands more than the expected 50%. Their effect sizes are smaller, and transmission comes disproportionately from mothers. This fits a **female protective effect**, in which females need a higher liability load to be diagnosed. Common-variant polygenic scores for autism explain a few percent of liability. They act additively with rare variants, and probands with a DNV still show over-transmitted polygenic risk, which supports a liability-threshold model.

**Mutational biology.** The paternal age effect reflects ongoing spermatogonial replication. A distinct phenomenon, **selfish spermatogonial selection**, affects genes such as *FGFR2*, *FGFR3*, *PTPN11* and *HRAS*. Gain-of-function mutations in these genes confer a clonal advantage within the testis, so their frequency rises steeply with age. Maternal age contributes modestly to DNVs, chiefly through clustered mutations, and strongly to aneuploidy.

**Nuance.** "De novo" is operationally defined from parental blood. Some apparent DNVs are actually low-level parental mosaicism, detectable in roughly 5-10% of cases with deep sequencing. This distinction materially changes recurrence estimates.

keyPoints: Inherited variants come from a parent; de novo variants arise new in the child
Each child carries ~60-70 de novo SNVs, about 1-2 in coding exons
Most DNVs are paternal and their number rises with father's age
Severe NDDs are enriched for de novo variants because selection removes them
Trio sequencing identifies DNVs by comparing child with both parents
Recurrence risk: ~1-2% de novo (germline mosaicism), 25% recessive, 50% inherited dominant

test.q: A de novo variant is best defined as one that:
choices: Passes from a carrier mother to her son
Is carried by both parents in a recessive pattern
Appears in the child but is absent in both parents
Is common in the population with small effect
test.explain: De novo means new: the variant is detected in the child but not in either parent's DNA.

test.q: Roughly how many de novo single-nucleotide variants does a typical child carry genome-wide?
test.explain: With a mutation rate near 1.2 x 10^-8 per base, each child gains roughly 60-70 DNVs. Only about 1-2 of them fall in coding exons.

test.q: Most de novo point mutations arise on which parent's chromosome?
test.explain: About 80% are paternal, because spermatogonia keep dividing throughout life.

test.q: Why are severe neurodevelopmental disorders enriched for de novo variants?
choices: De novo variants occur mainly in brain-expressed genes
Parents with variants usually lack any brain genes
Inherited variants are too large for DNA sequencing
Purifying selection removes strongly harmful inherited alleles
test.explain: Variants that greatly reduce reproduction are lost from the population quickly, so severe cases are maintained mostly by new mutations.

test.q: What is the usual sibling recurrence risk after an apparently de novo dominant variant?
test.explain: The risk is low but not zero. The residual risk comes from possible parental germline mosaicism.

test.q: Two carrier parents have a child with an autosomal recessive disorder. What is the risk in each further pregnancy?
test.explain: Each pregnancy has a 1 in 4 chance of inheriting both loss-of-function alleles.

test.q: Most children with Dravet syndrome carry a de novo variant in which gene?
test.explain: Dravet syndrome is mostly caused by de novo SCN1A variants, which affect a sodium channel in inhibitory neurons.

test.q: The 16p11.2 copy-number variant inherited from a mildly affected parent illustrates:
test.explain: The same variant can cause different severity in different family members, or may cause no clear phenotype at all.

test.q: Why does a de novo variant sometimes recur in a second child?
choices: The variant spreads from the first child
Common SNPs convert it to a dominant
test.explain: If some of a parent's eggs or sperm carry the variant, it can be passed on again even though parental blood tests negative.

test.q: Sequencing a child plus both parents is called what kind of analysis?
test.explain: Trio analysis lets labs spot variants present in the child but absent in both parents.

test.q: Many small effects of common variants are summed into a ___ risk score.
test.explain: Polygenic scores add up tiny effects from many common SNPs.

test.q: Which parent's age most strongly increases the number of de novo point mutations?
test.explain: Each extra year of paternal age adds roughly 1-2 de novo mutations.

kidTest.q: What does "de novo" mean?
kidTest.explain: De novo is Latin for new: the change appears for the first time in the child.

kidTest.q: Where do inherited instructions come from?
kidTest.explain: You get half from your mom and half from your dad.

kidTest.q: Why can one typo matter so much for the brain?
choices: The brain stops growing when you are born
The brain needs many instructions to grow right
The brain uses very few instructions
kidTest.explain: The brain needs thousands of instructions, so one important typo can change how it grows.

kidTest.q: If a child has a brand-new typo, will a later brother or sister usually have it?
kidTest.explain: The parents usually don't carry the typo, so later siblings usually won't have it.

kidTest.q: The giant instruction book in your body is called D _ _.
kidTest.explain: DNA holds the instructions for building your body and brain.

advancedTest.q: A gene shows de novo gain-of-function mutations whose frequency rises far faster with paternal age than the background rate. The best explanation is:
choices: Low-level postzygotic mosaicism in the child
Clonal advantage of mutant spermatogonia in the testis
Purifying selection acting against carrier fathers
Maternal clustered mutations at older ages
advancedTest.explain: Selfish spermatogonial selection (e.g., FGFR3, PTPN11) expands mutant clones over time, which exaggerates the paternal age effect.

advancedTest.q: Rare inherited truncating variants in constrained genes come disproportionately from unaffected mothers. This best supports:
choices: Purifying selection acting mainly on male carriers
Paternal germline mosaicism for each such allele
A female protective effect raising the liability threshold
Selfish selection of mutant oocytes in older mothers
advancedTest.explain: If females need more liability to be diagnosed, they can carry risk alleles without symptoms and pass them on to their children.

advancedTest.q: A child has a de novo variant, but parentage was never confirmed. Under ACMG/AMP criteria, this evidence is weighted as:
advancedTest.explain: Confirmed de novo status earns PS2. Assumed (unconfirmed) parentage is downgraded to PM6.

advancedTest.q: Deep sequencing finds a child's de novo variant in 3% of the father's sperm. Compared with the ~1% average, counselling should state that recurrence risk is:
choices: Lower than average, since blood was negative
Higher than average for this family
Unchanged, as the variant remains de novo
Zero, because the mother is the carrier
advancedTest.explain: Documented paternal germline mosaicism raises this family's individual recurrence risk well above the population average.

lessons.title: Somatic Mosaicism in the Brain

levels.kid:
Your body started as one tiny cell. That cell copied itself again and again to make trillions of cells. Each time it copied its instructions, called **DNA**, it was very careful. But once in a while, a tiny typo slipped in.

When a typo happens early, all the cells that come from that cell carry it too. So some cells have the typo and others do not. Scientists call this **mosaicism**, like a mosaic picture made of different colored tiles.

In the brain, a typo in just one patch of cells can sometimes change how that patch grows. This can cause seizures, which are like electrical storms in the brain. Doctors can sometimes help by finding and removing that one patch.
levels.hs:
**Somatic mosaicism** means that different cells in one person carry different DNA. It happens because DNA is copied every time a cell divides, and copying is not perfect. A change that arises after fertilization is called a **somatic variant** or **postzygotic variant**. It is passed only to that cell's descendants, not to every cell in the body.

Timing matters:
- A variant that arises very early in the embryo can end up in many tissues, including blood.
- A variant that arises later, in a brain **progenitor cell** (a cell that divides to make neurons), may be found only in one region of the brain.

Because the brain is built from progenitors that divide many times, every healthy brain is a mosaic. Most of these variants are harmless. But if a variant hits an important gene in the right cell at the right time, it can disrupt development.

A real example is **focal cortical dysplasia**, a patch of disorganized cortex that is a common cause of drug-resistant epilepsy in children. Many cases are caused by brain-only variants in genes of the **mTOR pathway**, such as *MTOR* itself. A standard blood test can miss these variants because blood cells do not carry them. Surgically removed brain tissue often reveals the cause.
levels.college:
Every neuron descends from the zygote through many rounds of division, so each carries a slightly different genome. **Somatic mosaicism** is the presence of genetically distinct cell populations in one individual because of postzygotic mutation.

**Types of somatic change in the brain**
- **SNVs**: single-nucleotide variants. Single-cell sequencing estimates that each human neuron carries on the order of a thousand or more somatic SNVs, and the count rises with age.
- **Copy-number changes and aneuploidy**: gains or losses of DNA segments or whole chromosomes in subsets of neurons.
- **Retrotransposition**: LINE-1 (L1) elements can copy and insert themselves in neural progenitors.

**Why timing determines the phenotype**
- An early variant can reach many lineages, so a high **variant allele fraction (VAF)** may show up in blood as well as brain.
- A late variant arising in a cortical progenitor stays confined to a clone of cells in one region. For a heterozygous variant, VAF in a tissue is about half the fraction of cells that carry it.

**Disease examples**
- **Focal cortical dysplasia type II** and **hemimegalencephaly** (overgrowth of one cerebral hemisphere): activating variants in *PIK3CA*, *AKT3* or *MTOR*. They over-activate mTORC1 and produce enlarged dysmorphic neurons.
- **Somatic second hits** in *DEPDC5*, *TSC1* or *TSC2* add to a germline variant.
- **Sturge-Weber syndrome**: a somatic *GNAQ* variant (R183Q) causes abnormal blood vessels in the brain and skin.
- **Mosaic tubulin and *DCX* variants** can cause milder neuronal migration defects than the full germline form.

**Detection**
Standard blood testing often misses brain-limited variants. Finding them requires deep sequencing of resected tissue, and sometimes of cell-free DNA. Somatic variants are not transmitted to offspring unless the germline is also involved, which changes recurrence-risk counseling.
levels.phd:
Mosaic variants carry their developmental history. In the brain they are both a disease mechanism and a natural lineage-tracing system.

**Mutation burden and processes.** Single-neuron whole-genome sequencing (Lodato et al., Science 2015; 2018) found that somatic SNVs accumulate with age at roughly 20 or more per neuron per year in the cortex. Their mutational signatures, dominated by clock-like C>T changes and transcription-coupled damage, point to mutation in post-mitotic neurons, not only replication error. Bae et al. (2018) estimated about 1.3 SNVs per cell division in early human neurogenesis. The predicted rise of L1 retrotransposition in neurons was later revised downward: single-cell estimates fell from many per cell to less than one per neuron (Evrony et al., 2012).

**Lineage reconstruction.** Shared clonal variants allowed phylogenies to be built across brain regions. Clones originating before gastrulation contribute to both hemispheres and non-neural tissues, which constrains models of how the cortex is allocated.

**The mTORopathy spectrum.** Phenotype follows both which gene is affected and when and where the variant arises:
- Hemimegalencephaly: VAFs often a few percent or higher, from an earlier origin.
- Focal cortical dysplasia II: often below 5%, sometimes below 1%, in dysmorphic neurons and balloon cells.
The **two-hit model** (germline *DEPDC5*/*NPRL2*/*NPRL3*/*TSC* loss plus a somatic second hit) explains focality in familial focal epilepsy. The **D'Gama et al. (2017)** and **Lim et al. (2015)** studies established brain-only *MTOR* variants. In mouse models, focal electroporation of such variants reproduced cortical lesions and seizures, and rapamycin rescued them.

**Nuance and controversy.**
- A low VAF can drive a network-level phenotype. A small dysmorphic clone appears to make the surrounding tissue epileptogenic, possibly through non-cell-autonomous effects.
- Distinguishing true low-VAF calls from sequencing artifacts (oxidative damage, PCR error) needs orthogonal validation.
- Excess somatic variants have been proposed for autism, schizophrenia and Alzheimer's disease. Effect sizes remain modest and debated, partly because studies of postmortem tissue are underpowered.
levels.expert:
Clinically, somatic mosaicism changes three things: which sample you test, how you interpret a negative result, and how you counsel the family.

**Sample choice.** For drug-resistant focal epilepsy with focal cortical dysplasia (FCD), hemimegalencephaly or polymicrogyria, a negative blood exome does not exclude a genetic cause. Sequence fresh-frozen resected tissue with deep targeted panels (often over 500x) or ultra-deep amplicon sequencing. Formalin-fixed tissue yields more artifactual C>T calls. Diagnostic yield in FCD II from tissue is roughly 30-60% for mTOR pathway genes, and is higher when dysmorphic neurons are enriched, for example by laser capture or nuclei sorting. Brain-predominant variants are increasingly found in *SLC35A2* in mild malformation of cortical development with oligodendroglial hyperplasia in epilepsy (MOGHE). Tissue from the trajectories of stereo-EEG electrodes, and the cerebrospinal fluid, are emerging minimally invasive sources, though yields are variable.

**Surgical implications.** Because the epileptogenic clone may extend beyond the MRI-visible lesion, residual variant-positive tissue at the resection margin has been linked to persistent seizures. This argues for complete resection guided by stereo-EEG. Several groups are exploring intraoperative or margin genotyping.

**Precision therapy.** Confirming mTORC1 hyperactivation supports an mTOR inhibitor. Everolimus has trial evidence in tuberous sclerosis complex (EXIST-3). Its benefit in isolated FCD is less established. Alpelisib, a PI3Kα inhibitor, is used in *PIK3CA*-related overgrowth spectrum, and its effects on the brain are under study.

**Pitfalls.**
- A low VAF in blood can mean the parent is mosaic. Test the parents with sensitive methods before quoting a near-zero recurrence risk.
- Clonal hematopoiesis in older individuals can mimic constitutional mosaicism in blood.
- Variants of uncertain significance at low VAF need functional context, such as phospho-S6 staining, before they can be called causal.

**Open questions.** Does somatic burden contribute meaningfully to common neuropsychiatric risk? Can noninvasive liquid biopsy reliably detect brain clones? And could early, clone-targeted therapy prevent epileptogenesis rather than merely suppress seizures?

keyPoints: Somatic (postzygotic) variants make each brain a genetic mosaic
Timing of a variant determines how widespread it is
Brain-only mTOR pathway variants cause FCD II and hemimegalencephaly
Blood testing can miss brain-limited variants; test resected tissue
Variant allele fraction reflects the share of cells carrying a variant
Mosaicism changes therapy choice and recurrence-risk counseling

test.q: Somatic mosaicism means:
choices: A child inherits DNA from both parents
Two separate embryos fuse into one person
Cells within one person carry different DNA
Body cells share one identical genome
test.explain: Postzygotic variants create genetically distinct cell populations within one individual. Fusion of two embryos is chimerism, which is a different process.

test.q: Why might a blood test miss the cause of focal cortical dysplasia?
choices: Blood cells lack the mTOR pathway genes
Brain disorders are not caused by DNA changes
Blood DNA degrades too fast to be read
The variant may exist in brain cells but not blood
test.explain: A variant that arose later, in a brain progenitor, is confined to brain tissue, so blood cells do not carry it.

test.q: A variant arising very early in the embryo is most likely to:
choices: Spread to many tissues, including blood
Appear just in sperm or egg cells
test.explain: Early variants are passed to many cell lineages, so they can appear in many tissues.

test.q: Brain-only variants in FCD type II mostly affect which pathway?
test.explain: Activating variants in genes such as *MTOR*, *PIK3CA* and *AKT3* over-activate mTORC1, which produces dysmorphic neurons.

test.q: Hemimegalencephaly is best described as:
test.explain: Hemimegalencephaly is enlargement of one hemisphere, often caused by somatic mTOR pathway variants.

test.q: Sturge-Weber syndrome is caused by a somatic variant in:
test.explain: A somatic *GNAQ* R183Q variant causes the abnormal blood vessels seen in Sturge-Weber syndrome.

test.q: In the two-hit model of focal epilepsy, the second hit is:
choices: An infection that damages the cortex
A somatic variant on top of a germline one
A head injury that occurs during childhood
A second germline variant from the other parent
test.explain: A germline loss-of-function variant (for example in *DEPDC5*) plus a somatic second hit in brain cells explains why lesions are focal.

test.q: If 10% of cells carry a heterozygous variant, the expected VAF is about:
test.explain: Each heterozygous cell carries one variant copy out of two, so VAF is about half the fraction of carrier cells.

test.q: What can LINE-1 elements do in neural progenitors?
test.explain: L1 retrotransposons can copy and insert themselves into new places in the genome, which adds to somatic diversity.

test.q: A variant that arises after fertilization is also called a post___ variant.
test.explain: Postzygotic means arising after the zygote forms, so the variant is not present in every cell.

test.q: What abbreviation describes the fraction of sequencing reads carrying a variant?
test.explain: The variant allele fraction (VAF) estimates how many cells carry a variant.

test.q: Focal cortical ___ is a patch of disorganized cortex causing drug-resistant epilepsy.
test.explain: Focal cortical dysplasia is often caused by brain-limited mTOR pathway variants.

kidTest.q: What is a mosaic in your body?
kidTest.explain: Like tiles of different colors, some of your cells carry a DNA typo and others do not.

kidTest.q: When can a DNA typo slip in?
choices: When a cell copies its DNA
kidTest.explain: Copying DNA is very careful, but once in a while it makes a mistake.

kidTest.q: What can a typo in one brain patch cause?
kidTest.explain: A patch that grew differently can cause electrical storms called seizures.

kidTest.q: How can doctors sometimes help with that patch?
kidTest.explain: Surgery can sometimes take out the patch that causes the seizures.

kidTest.q: The instructions inside your cells are called D _ _.
kidTest.explain: DNA holds the instructions that cells copy when they divide.

advancedTest.q: Hemimegalencephaly usually shows a higher VAF than FCD II. The best explanation is:
choices: The variant arose earlier, in a larger progenitor pool
Hemimegalencephaly variants are inherited from a parent
FCD II variants are removed by immune clearance
Larger brain tissue samples inflate the allele counts
advancedTest.explain: An earlier origin gives a larger clone and a wider lesion. FCD II arises from later, smaller clones, so its VAF is lower.

advancedTest.q: Persistent seizures after a lesionectomy with variant-positive margins suggest:
choices: The seizures arose from a germline cause
The variant was a sequencing artifact
The surgery triggered a new mutation
The clone extended beyond the visible lesion
advancedTest.explain: The epileptogenic clone can extend past the MRI-visible lesion, so the tissue left at the margin can keep driving seizures.

advancedTest.q: A child's de novo variant appears at 8% VAF in a parent's blood. The key implication is:
choices: The child's variant is likely brain-limited
Recurrence risk exceeds the baseline estimate
The child's recurrence risk is near zero
The parent likely has clonal hematopoiesis
advancedTest.explain: A parent who is mosaic may also carry the variant in the germline, which raises recurrence risk above a near-zero estimate.

advancedTest.q: Clock-like C>T signatures in single neurons support the view that somatic SNVs:
choices: Accumulate in post-mitotic neurons with age
advancedTest.explain: Age-linked accumulation and transcription-coupled signatures indicate mutation in non-dividing neurons, not only replication errors during development.

lessons.title: Haploinsufficiency, Dominant-Negative and Gain-of-Function Effects

levels.kid:
You have two copies of almost every gene, one from mom and one from dad. Each copy is like a recipe card for making a tiny machine in your body.

Sometimes one card has a mistake. What happens next depends on the kind of mistake.

- **Not enough**: one card is torn up, so the body makes only half the machines. For some brain jobs, half is not enough.
- **The spoiler**: the broken machine joins the good ones and jams them, like one wrong puzzle piece ruining a whole puzzle.
- **Too strong**: the machine works too hard, like a light switch stuck on.

The brain is very picky. It needs just the right amount of each machine. That is why doctors care which kind of mistake it is.
levels.hs:
Most genes come in two copies, called **alleles**. A disorder is **dominant** when changing just one allele causes it. There are three main ways one bad copy can do this.

- **Haploinsufficiency**: one copy is lost or broken (a **loss-of-function** variant), and the remaining copy makes only about 50% of the protein. For dosage-sensitive genes, 50% is not enough.
- **Dominant-negative**: the faulty protein is still made, and it interferes with the normal protein. This usually happens when proteins work in teams, such as channels built from several subunits.
- **Gain-of-function**: the altered protein does something too much, too long, or something new.

A real example is the sodium channel gene **SCN1A**. Losing one copy causes **Dravet syndrome**, a severe childhood epilepsy. The loss mainly weakens inhibitory neurons, the cells that act as the brain's brakes.

A related gene, **SCN2A**, shows that the type of effect matters. Gain-of-function SCN2A variants cause seizures starting in the first months of life. Loss-of-function SCN2A variants more often cause autism or intellectual disability, sometimes with later seizures.

The brain is especially sensitive to gene dosage. Neurons depend on precisely balanced signals, so small shifts in protein amount or activity can change how circuits develop.
levels.college:
When a heterozygous variant causes disease, the **mechanism** describes how one altered allele perturbs function.

**Haploinsufficiency (HI)**
- Caused by null alleles: nonsense, frameshift, canonical splice-site variants, or whole-gene deletions.
- Premature stop codons usually trigger **nonsense-mediated decay (NMD)**, so the mutant mRNA is degraded and little or no mutant protein is made.
- HI genes in neurodevelopment include **SCN1A**, **SYNGAP1**, **SHANK3**, **CHD8**, **ARID1B** and **FOXP1**. Many are transcription regulators, chromatin remodelers or synaptic scaffolds, where stoichiometry matters.

**Dominant-negative (DN)**
- A stable mutant protein poisons complexes it joins.
- Typical in multimers. Voltage-gated potassium channels such as **KCNQ2** form tetramers, so one mutant subunit can impair a channel containing normal subunits.
- If subunits assemble randomly, only (1/2)^4 ≈ 6% of tetramers are fully wild-type. Activity can therefore fall well below 50%.

**Gain-of-function (GoF)**
- Usually missense variants that increase or prolong activity or create a new property.
- Examples: **SCN8A** GoF variants that increase persistent sodium current and cause early-onset epileptic encephalopathy, and activating **GRIN2A/GRIN2B** NMDA receptor variants.
- Toxic GoF also includes expanded repeats that produce toxic RNA or protein. That topic is covered elsewhere.

**Why it matters**
- Variant type predicts mechanism. Truncating variants spread along a gene suggest HI. Clustered, recurrent missense variants suggest GoF or DN.
- Opposite mechanisms in one gene can need opposite treatments. Sodium channel blockers can help SCN2A or SCN8A GoF epilepsy, but they worsen Dravet syndrome caused by SCN1A loss.
levels.phd:
Dosage sensitivity can be estimated from population data. **gnomAD** constraint metrics such as **pLI** and **LOEUF** (loss-of-function observed/expected upper bound fraction) measure depletion of protein-truncating variants in healthy people. Genes with a low LOEUF tolerate heterozygous loss poorly and are strongly enriched among autism and developmental disorder genes. The **ClinGen** dosage curation assigns HI and triplosensitivity scores. Some genes, such as **MECP2**, are sensitive in both directions. MECP2 loss causes Rett syndrome in females, and duplication causes MECP2 duplication syndrome in males.

Why are neurons so sensitive to dosage? Several ideas are proposed:
- **Threshold effects** in transcriptional networks, where a transcription factor at half dose falls below the occupancy needed at low-affinity enhancers.
- **Chromatin regulators** whose effects accumulate through development.
- **Excitation–inhibition balance**. In the Scn1a+/− mouse (Yu et al., 2006, Catterall lab), loss of Nav1.1 selectively reduced sodium current and firing in GABAergic interneurons. This explained why losing a sodium channel produces hyperexcitability.

**Dominant-negative** effects depend on assembly. With random assembly of an n-mer, the fraction of fully wild-type complexes is (1/2)^n. Proteins forming larger homomeric complexes are enriched for DN variants. Structural studies show that DN and GoF missense variants are less destabilizing than recessive loss-of-function missense variants. A protein that is too unstable to fold cannot poison a complex. As a result, stability predictors such as FoldX systematically miss non-loss-of-function mechanisms (Gerasimavicius et al., 2022).

**Gain-of-function** is diverse. It includes hypermorphs (increased normal activity), neomorphs (new activity), and altered gating, such as shifted voltage dependence or slowed inactivation.

The categories are not always clean. In **KCNQ2**, DN variants with near-total loss of M-current cause encephalopathy. Milder loss-of-function variants cause self-limited familial neonatal epilepsy, and rare GoF variants cause a distinct phenotype. Electrophysiology, ideally using co-expression with wild-type subunits, is needed to assign mechanism.
levels.expert:
In the clinic, assigning a mechanism is a step in variant interpretation, not an afterthought. Under ACMG/AMP criteria, **PVS1** (null variant) applies only when loss of function is an established disease mechanism for that gene. Applying it to a gene whose disease is driven by GoF is a common error. The ClinGen SVI decision tree also asks whether a truncating variant escapes NMD. Variants in the last exon, or within about 50 nucleotides of the final exon junction, can produce truncated proteins that act as DN or GoF.

Mechanism now drives therapy design:
- **Haploinsufficiency** suits upregulating the healthy allele. **Zorevunersen** (STK-001) is an antisense oligonucleotide that uses TANGO to block a nonproductive poison exon in SCN1A transcripts and raise Nav1.1. It has reduced seizure frequency in trials. Other approaches include CRISPR activation (dCas9-based) and AAV-delivered regulatory elements such as ETX101.
- **GoF** suits knockdown. Allele-nonselective ASOs against SCN2A or SCN8A are in clinical development. Simple knockdown risks pushing a dosage-sensitive gene into haploinsufficiency, so the therapeutic window is narrow.
- **DN** is the hardest. Simply adding wild-type protein dilutes the poison but may not overcome it. Allele-specific silencing combined with replacement, or base editing of the mutant allele, is often needed.

Pitfalls:
- Heterologous expression systems such as HEK cells or oocytes can mislabel variants. A variant can be GoF at one level, such as current density, and loss-of-function at another, such as neuronal firing. SCN2A variants with mixed properties are an example.
- Mosaic parents and incomplete penetrance complicate segregation evidence.
- Patient-derived iPSC neurons and human cortical organoids are increasingly used to test mechanism in a human cellular context.

Open questions include how to predict mechanism from sequence at scale, and when in development dosage correction must happen. Rescue in adult mouse models of **Syngap1** and **Shank3** has been partial and age-dependent, which suggests critical windows. Variant-effect models such as AlphaMissense predict pathogenicity, but they do not yet classify mechanism. Deep mutational scanning of neuronal channels is beginning to fill this gap.

keyPoints: Haploinsufficiency: one lost copy leaves ~50% protein, too little for dosage-sensitive genes
Dominant-negative: a mutant protein poisons complexes, so activity can fall below 50%
Gain-of-function: the protein is overactive, prolonged or newly active
Truncating variants and NMD suggest loss of function; clustered missense suggests GoF or DN
SCN1A loss causes Dravet syndrome by weakening inhibitory interneurons
Mechanism guides therapy: upregulate for HI, knock down for GoF

test.q: Haploinsufficiency means disease results because:
choices: Both copies of the gene are deleted
One working copy gives too little protein
The protein gains a new toxic activity
A mutant protein jams normal partners
test.explain: In haploinsufficiency, about 50% of the protein is not enough for normal function. Losing both copies would be a recessive situation.

test.q: Dominant-negative effects are most typical of proteins that:
choices: Are secreted into the blood plasma
Are made mainly in early embryos
test.explain: A mutant subunit can poison a complex such as a tetrameric channel. This impairs the normal subunits it assembles with.

test.q: Loss of one SCN1A copy causes which disorder?
test.explain: SCN1A haploinsufficiency causes Dravet syndrome, a severe childhood epilepsy.

test.q: Why does losing a sodium channel in Dravet syndrome cause seizures?
choices: Excitatory neurons fire far more often
Neurons gain a new calcium channel
test.explain: Nav1.1 loss mainly weakens GABAergic interneurons, the brain's brakes, which tips circuits toward hyperexcitability.

test.q: A premature stop codon usually leads to loss of function because the mRNA undergoes:
test.explain: NMD degrades transcripts with premature stops, so little or no mutant protein is made.

test.q: With random assembly, about what fraction of tetrameric channels are fully wild-type in a heterozygote?
test.explain: (1/2)^4 is about 6%, so a dominant-negative variant can drop activity far below 50%.

test.q: Which variant pattern most suggests gain-of-function?
choices: Recurrent missense clustered in a domain
test.explain: Clustered, recurrent missense variants suggest a specific functional change. Scattered truncating variants suggest haploinsufficiency.

test.q: Why are sodium channel blockers avoided in Dravet syndrome?
choices: They raise sodium channel expression too much
They block GABA receptors in interneurons
They are toxic mainly to the liver in children
They further reduce already low Nav1.1 function
test.explain: Dravet syndrome is a loss of function, so blocking sodium channels worsens it. Blockers can help gain-of-function SCN2A or SCN8A epilepsy.

test.q: Gain-of-function SCN2A variants typically cause:
test.explain: SCN2A GoF variants cause early-infantile seizures. Loss-of-function variants more often cause autism or intellectual disability.

test.q: Each of the two copies of a gene is called an ___.
test.explain: Alleles are alternative copies of a gene, one inherited from each parent.

test.q: Which potassium channel gene forms tetramers and shows dominant-negative variants in neonatal encephalopathy?
test.explain: KCNQ2 subunits form tetramers, so a mutant subunit can poison channels containing normal subunits.

test.q: A variant that removes a gene's normal activity is called a loss-of-___ variant.
test.explain: Loss-of-function variants include nonsense, frameshift and deletion alleles.

kidTest.q: How many copies of most genes do you have?
kidTest.explain: You get one copy from mom and one from dad.

kidTest.q: In the 'not enough' problem, what happens?
choices: The body makes half the machines
The machines work far too hard
The machines turn into new cells
kidTest.explain: One card is torn up, so only half as many machines get made.

kidTest.q: What does the 'spoiler' machine do?
kidTest.explain: Like a wrong puzzle piece, it messes up the good ones.

kidTest.q: A 'too strong' machine is like:
kidTest.explain: It keeps working when it should stop.

kidTest.q: Which body part is very picky about having the right amount of each machine? (b _ _ _ _)
kidTest.explain: The brain needs just the right amount of each machine to work well.

advancedTest.q: A last-exon nonsense variant appears in a gene whose disease mechanism is gain-of-function. What is the best interpretation?
choices: It may escape NMD, so PVS1 is not automatically valid
Apply PVS1 because nonsense variants are reliably null
Assume haploinsufficiency because the gene is dosage-sensitive
Classify it as benign because truncations cause no GoF
advancedTest.explain: Last-exon truncations can escape NMD and produce active proteins. PVS1 also requires loss of function to be the established disease mechanism.

advancedTest.q: Why do stability predictors such as FoldX underperform for dominant-negative missense variants?
choices: DN variants tend to be mildly destabilizing so they still assemble
DN proteins are degraded faster than wild-type proteins
DN variants occur mostly in noncoding regulatory DNA
Stability tools model membrane proteins poorly in general
advancedTest.explain: A mutant protein has to fold and assemble to poison a complex. Highly destabilizing variants behave as simple loss of function instead.

advancedTest.q: Why is allele-nonselective ASO knockdown for SCN2A GoF epilepsy risky?
choices: Too much knockdown could create a haploinsufficiency phenotype
It converts the variant into a dominant-negative allele
It increases persistent sodium current further
ASOs are poorly taken up by cortical neurons
advancedTest.explain: SCN2A is also sensitive to loss of function. Overshooting the knockdown can shift a patient toward the autism and intellectual disability spectrum.

advancedTest.q: MECP2 shows disease with both loss and duplication. This implies the gene is:
choices: Free of dosage constraint in populations
Sensitive to both too little and too much dosage
Haploinsufficient but tolerant of extra copies
advancedTest.explain: MECP2 loss causes Rett syndrome and duplication causes MECP2 duplication syndrome. This means the gene is sensitive to dosage in both directions, which ClinGen scores as both HI and triplosensitivity.
